Ep 209 of Facts vs Feelings is here!

The bull market turned four this week 🎂

@sonusvarghese and I dig into what's driving it and where the stress is building

📈 The S&P 500 is up about 118% since October 2022, or 131% with dividends. Every bull market in the last 50 years that reached its third birthday went on to see a fifth.

💰 Profit growth accounts for roughly 85 points of the gain, about 40 of them from margin expansion. This year the forward P/E fell from about 22x to 19.5x as Treasury yields climbed, and earnings growth more than offset it.

💳 CCC spreads are near 900 bps. High yield overall is flat, and rate-hedged high yield and loans are beating cash. Ryan and Sonu see a duration problem from rising yields.

🏦 Hyperscaler bonds went from 1-2% of net new Treasury borrowing to about 14% in a year. SpaceX raised roughly $150B in four months, and its five-year CDS hit a record 200 bps.

🤖 Billions in AI compute contracts start billing between 2027 and 2029. Sonu flags 2027 and 2028 as the potential reckoning for the AI capex cycle.

We also cover small caps vs higher yields, the dollar back above 100 on the DXY, and next week's midterm episode with PIMCO's Libby Cantrell.

👇👇

Now that AI agents can own an outcome from start to finish, how do you sell them?

1. Sell the platform:

License the agent to a company to run in its own operations. No existing contract sets the price, so there's more upside, but new budgets take time to approve and results are harder to credit to the agent.

2. Sell the service:

Take over work a company already outsources, the way Red Ventures sold policies for insurers and got paid per policy closed. The budget already exists, so deals close faster, but the highest-value work usually runs in-house, which caps the upside.

3. Go full-stack:

Become the business, like buying debt portfolios and collecting on them yourself. You keep all the value the AI creates, but you also take on the licensing and compliance.

Any crack in its architecture is maybe even more damaging to its value than the less sophisticated privacy protocols out there, because suddenly it's not the perfect solution anymore.
It's true that it would still be a viable blockchain with a great development community underneath, but losing its USP would be severe in my eyes and that is why I have adjusted my risk. I do expect there will be others out there who do not take that view, but that is any speculative market; it is an aggregate of all of these understandings. If you have read my other writings you will know I am no longer a fan of Bitcoin (and its "money" narrative) given its current state. This is also why I have encouraged ZSAs to be implemented. Onchain revenue and anonymity sets are two very important moats for a protocol's standing in the industry.

In the drawdown from last year’s highs, SUI fell about 80%, SOL about 70%, ETH about 60%. Brutal.

But the charts missed what was underneath. On all three, economic density didn’t move. Users left, as they always do in a bear market, but the capital each remaining user had deployed stayed exactly where it was... the tourists and the bots went, and the people who stayed kept doing what they’d been doing.

I spent a lot of time measuring this: stablecoin float, DeFi TVL and applications shipped per daily user, across every major L1. Why? Because I think it’s the truest measure of longevity there is.

Every other L1 I measured lost density along with price. Adoption hadn’t taken hold yet. Doesn’t mean it won’t, but it hasn’t...

i wanted a physical version of my ai agent. Something real in the living room that shows my to-do list and my day, and that my wife can see too.

I bought a seeed reterminal e1002, an e-ink display. e-ink because it looks like paper: no glow, no buzz, it just sits there like a note on the wall (almost)

setup was honestly simple:
- built the open-source muse gadget firmware on my computer with my sdk token in it
- flashed it to the device over usb
- paired it in the muse app (settings, devices, developer mode) thanks @natfriedman 

now every morning at 7am my agent renders my briefing (calendar, top to-dos, weather) and pushes it to the screen. my wife reads it over coffee. it basically became the family's shared to-do list

whole thing took ~20 min. your agent doesn't have to live in a chat window. give it a physical representation!
